In algebraic geometry, given a [[morphism of schemes]] <math>p: X \to S</math>, the '''diagonal morphism'''
:<math>\delta: X \to X \times_S X</math>
is a morphism determined by the [[universal property]] of the [[fiber product of schemes|fiber product]] <math>X \times_S X</math> of ''p'' and ''p'' applied to the identity <math>1_X : X \to X</math> and the identity <math>1_X</math>.

It is a special case of a [[graph morphism (algebraic geometry)|graph morphism]]: given a morphism <math>f: X \to Y</math> over ''S'', the graph morphism of it is <math>X \to X \times_S Y</math> induced by <math>f</math> and the identity <math>1_X</math>. The diagonal embedding is the graph morphism of <math>1_X</math>.

By definition, ''X'' is a '''separated scheme''' over ''S'' (<math>p: X \to S</math> is a '''separated morphism''') if the diagonal morphism is a [[closed immersion]]. Also, a morphism <math>p: X \to S</math> locally of finite presentation is an [[unramified morphism]] [[if and only if]] the diagonal embedding is an open immersion.

== Explanation ==
As an example, consider an [[algebraic variety]] over an [[algebraically closed field]] ''k'' and <math>p: X \to \operatorname{Spec}(k)</math> the structure map. Then, identifying ''X'' with the set of its ''k''-rational points, <math>X \times_k X = \{ (x, y) \in X \times X \}</math> and <math>\delta: X \to X \times_k X</math> is given as <math>x \mapsto (x, x)</math>; whence the name diagonal morphism.

== Separated morphism ==
A '''separated morphism''' is a morphism <math> f </math> such that the [[fiber product]] of <math> f </math> with itself along <math> f </math> has its [[diagonal]] as a closed subscheme &mdash; in other words, the diagonal morphism is a ''closed immersion''.

As a consequence, a scheme <math> X </math> is '''separated''' when the diagonal of <math> X </math> within the ''scheme product'' of <math> X </math> with itself is a closed immersion. Emphasizing the relative point of view, one might equivalently define a scheme to be separated if the unique morphism <math>X \rightarrow \textrm{Spec} (\mathbb{Z})</math> is separated.

Notice that a [[topological space]] ''Y'' is [[Hausdorff topological space|Hausdorff]] iff the diagonal embedding 
:<math>Y \stackrel{\Delta}{\longrightarrow} Y \times Y, \, y \mapsto (y, y)</math>
is closed. In algebraic geometry, the above formulation is used because a scheme which is a Hausdorff space is necessarily empty or zero-dimensional. The difference between the topological and algebro-geometric context comes from the topological structure of the fiber product (in the category of schemes) <math>X \times_{\textrm{Spec} (\mathbb{Z})} X</math>, which is different from the product of topological spaces.

Any ''affine'' scheme ''Spec A'' is separated, because the diagonal corresponds to the surjective map of rings (hence is a closed immersion of schemes):
:''<math>A \otimes_{\mathbb Z} A \rightarrow A, a \otimes a' \mapsto a \cdot a'</math>''.

Let <math>S</math> be a scheme obtained by identifying two affine lines through the [[Identity function|identity map]] except at the origins (see [[gluing scheme#Examples]]). It is not separated.<ref>{{harvnb|Hartshorne|1977|loc=Example 4.0.1.}}</ref> Indeed, the image of the diagonal morphism <math>S \to S \times S</math> image has two origins, while its closure contains four origins.

== Use in intersection theory ==
A classic way to define the [[intersection product]] of [[Algebraic cycle|algebraic cycles]] <math>A, B</math> on a [[smooth variety]] ''X'' is by intersecting (restricting) their cartesian product with (to) the diagonal: precisely,
:<math>A \cdot B = \delta^*(A \times B)</math>
where <math>\delta^*</math> is the pullback along the diagonal embedding <math>\delta: X \to X \times X</math>.
